title: Wonton Soup
subtitle: Pork and prawn wontons in a clear, aromatic chicken broth
excerpt: Pork and prawn wontons are folded in thin wrappers and cooked in a clear chicken broth seasoned with ginger, soy sauce and sesame oil. The soup is clean, aromatic and deeply satisfying. Serves 4 in about 60 minutes, including folding the wontons. Freeze uncooked wontons for a much faster version on future evenings.
sourceNotes: Wonton soup is one of the most widely eaten noodle soups in Cantonese cooking and is particularly associated with the street food of Hong Kong and Guangzhou. The dish appears in Eileen Yin-Fei Lo's 'The Chinese Kitchen' (William Morrow, 1999), which covers the technique in detail, and in Yan-Kit So's 'Classic Food of China' (Macmillan, 1992), which traces the wonton's history in southern Chinese cooking and distinguishes the Cantonese soup version from the Sichuan version served in chilli oil.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked wontons on a lined tray until solid, then transfer to a bag for up to 3 months. Cook from frozen directly in simmering water for 6 to 7 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made up to 24 hours ahead. The broth can be made up to 3 days ahead and kept in the fridge.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thin squares of egg-enriched wheat dough, sold fresh or frozen in Chinese grocery shops. They are thinner and more elastic than dumpling skins and turn silky when boiled. Square wrappers are used for wontons; round wrappers are usually for gyoza-style dumplings.

In Chinese cooking, a clear broth is a stock that has been made without heavy browning of the bones, producing a pale, clean-tasting liquid. For wonton soup, a good clear broth is the backbone of the dish. It should taste of chicken and ginger without being overpowering, so the delicate flavour of the wontons comes through.

The folding technique used to seal wontons. The most common home method folds the square wrapper into a triangle, then brings the two far corners together and presses them to join, creating a small packet with a ruffled top. This shape is sometimes called a nurse's cap or gold ingot, and it traps a little pocket of the filling that stays juicy when cooked.

A Chinese fermented rice wine named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. It has a rich, slightly nutty flavour and is used in marinades and sauces throughout Chinese cooking. In wonton filling it removes the rawness from the pork and prawn mixture. Dry sherry makes a reasonable substitute.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 60 minutes in total, most of which is folding the wontons. Once you have a batch in the freezer, the dish takes about 20 minutes from start to finish on subsequent evenings. The
is as important as the wontons: a good homemade stock or a good-quality bought stock both work, but water with a stock cube will produce a thin, unsatisfying result.
step is the most time-consuming part. Use
rather than dumpling skins: they are thinner and cook through more quickly. Keep the wrappers covered with a damp cloth while you work, as they dry out and crack within minutes.

Combine the {{pork-mince}}, {{raw-prawns}}, {{ginger}}, {{spring-onions}}, {{shaoxing-wine}}, soy sauce, sesame oil, white pepper and sugar. Stir in one direction for 1 minute until the mixture holds together. Cover and refrigerate while you prepare the wrappers.

Set out the {{wonton-wrappers}} with a small bowl of water. Place a rounded teaspoon of filling in the centre. Wet two edges of the wrapper with a damp finger. Fold to form a triangle and press out any air, sealing firmly. Bring the two base corners of the triangle together, wet one and press to join. Place on a lightly floured tray and cover with a damp cloth.

While folding the wontons, prepare the broth. Combine the {{chicken-stock}} and sliced ginger in a saucepan and bring to a simmer. Season with soy sauce, sesame oil and salt. Keep warm over a low heat.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the wontons in two batches. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring gently once, until they float and the filling is cooked through. Lift out with a slotted spoon.
Divide the wontons between four deep bowls. Ladle the hot broth over them, add a pinch of white pepper and top with sliced spring onions. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The wontons are bursting open in the boiling water
items.cause: Too much filling or the seal was not pressed firmly enough
items.fix: Use no more than a rounded teaspoon of filling. Press all air out before sealing and check each wonton is completely closed before it goes in the water.

items.symptom: The broth tastes thin and flat
items.cause: The stock was weak or over-diluted
items.fix: Use less water in the broth or reduce the stock slightly before adding the seasoning. Add a splash of extra soy sauce and taste before ladling.

items.symptom: The wonton wrappers are tearing when being folded
items.fix: Keep unused wrappers covered with a damp cloth. Work faster, or dampen the wrappers slightly with a wet finger before folding if they have already dried.

content.text: Wonton soup is one of the defining dishes of Cantonese street food. In Hong Kong, wonton noodle soup shops, known as mian jia, serve it with thin egg noodles in a broth made from dried shrimp roe and pork bones that has been simmering for hours. The home version uses a simpler chicken broth but keeps the same balance: delicate wontons in a clean, well-seasoned soup. The
in the filling is what gives the pork and prawn mixture its depth, and a batch in the freezer means wonton soup is always less than 20 minutes away.
